newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Indonesia says Lisbon blocks new ASEAN-EU pact.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says Lisbon blocks new ASEAN-EU pact.

text.p: Portugal is blocking a new treaty between Europe and Southeast Asia over the issue of East Timor, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said on Thursday.

He said the Portuguese had so far not brought up Indonesia's occupation of the former Portuguese colony at a meeting between the European Union (EU) and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).

A Portuguese diplomat said, however, the 15-member European Union would bring up East Timor in closed-door talks among the foreign ministers but it would not be put on the formal agenda and would not be mentioned in the final declaration.

Alatas said Lisbon was blocking plans to sign a treaty formalising a new level of relations between the EU and the seven ASEAN members -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

"(East Timor) was one of the issues used by Portugal to prevent a new-generation agreement to be signed by the two sides and of course we deeply regret it," Alatas told reporters after the foreign ministers met on Thursday.
"Right now, we're cooperating on the basis of the old agreement with some modifications," he said.
A senior ASEAN official told Reuters the new agreement, which would have treaty status, required the signatures of all members, something Portugal has refused to give.
But he said a final declaration from the meeting, expected to be adopted on Friday, would contain many of the projects envisioned in the treaty.
Alatas said Indonesia was willing to discuss the East Timor issue with Portugal at the appropriate forum.

"Our position has always been that we are most willing to discuss it in the appropriate forum. We've never been afraid, we've never shrunk from discussing this with Portugal in any other forum which is appropriate."
Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama told reporters Lisbon also wanted talks.

"As you know, the European Union is quite concerned about the human rights situation in East Timor," he said. "And the EU wants...a comprehensive and internationally accepted solution to the East Timor problem."

Pakistan's former U.N. envoy, Jamsheed Marker, was appointed on Wednesday as U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan's personal representative for East Timor to help in talks that have dragged on for almost 15 years.
The United Nations has never recognised Indonesia's 1976 annexation of East Timor, which it invaded the previous year after the departure of Portugal, the colonial power.
Talks to find an internationally acceptable solution were initiated by then-Secretary-General Javier Perez de Cuellar in 1983 and continued by his successor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Alatas said there were no plans to meet his Portuguese counterpart on the sidelines of the ASEAN-EU meeting or anywhere else in the near future.
"We'll have to wait when we can restart the negotiations, an indication from the secretary-general when discussions can resume," Alatas said.
"We have always stated we'll cooperate with the secretary-general to find a just and comprehensive solution."
